It had no holdfast and probably lay on the soft sea floor with its tip in the mud, catching small prey with its tentacles.

A big, smooth-shelled asaphid trilobite from the Late Ordovician seas that covered what is now Ohio, Indiana and Kentucky, recognised by its broad semicircular head and tail shields and backswept cheek spines. Complete specimens reach at least 53 cm. Isotelus, best known from this species, has been Ohio's official state fossil since 1985.

The largest complete trilobite ever found: the holotype, from Late Ordovician rocks near Churchill in northern Manitoba, is 72 cm long. Its smooth, elongate oval shield lacks cheek spines. It lived in warm, shallow tropical seas and probably ploughed through the seafloor sediment hunting and scavenging soft-bodied prey.

The type species of Isotelus, described in 1824 from the Trenton rocks of New York and found across much of Middle and Late Ordovician North America. It is slimmer and flatter than Isotelus maximus, with more triangular head and tail shields, and adults have no cheek spines. Most specimens are 20-25 cm long, though some grow to nearly twice that.

A small blind trilobite, usually 2-4 cm long, from Ordovician mudstones of Wales and the Welsh Borderland, and the type species of its genus. Its swollen head is ringed by a broad fringe pierced by concentric rows of pits, and long spines trail behind it. Nobody is sure what the fringe was for: ideas include sifting food from the sediment, sensing the water, and keeping the animal from sinking into soft mud.

A small fringed trilobite from the Late Ordovician of Scandinavia, especially Norway and Sweden. It is now usually placed in the genus Tretaspis, of which it is the type species. A raised ridge splits its pitted fringe into outer and inner bands; it has small eye bumps but probably could not see, and its very long, thin cheek spines inspired the name 'seticornis', meaning 'bristle-horned'.

A North Pacific baleen whale up to about 14 m long that feeds mostly on the seafloor: it rolls onto its side, sucks up mouthfuls of sediment and strains out amphipods and other small invertebrates through its short, pale baleen. Its mottled grey skin is crusted with barnacles and whale lice, and it has a low hump and a row of knuckles instead of a dorsal fin. Eastern Pacific grey whales make one of the longest migrations of any mammal, between Arctic feeding grounds and the warm lagoons of Baja California where their calves are born.

The largest known sabre-toothed cat, a heavily built predator of Pleistocene South America estimated at about 220-400 kg, with upper canines up to about 28 cm long. Its massive forelimbs probably pinned large prey while the long, flattened sabres delivered a deep bite to the throat. It disappeared at the end of the Pleistocene, about 10,000 years ago.

The earliest and smallest species of Smilodon, roughly the size of a jaguar at about 55-100 kg. It lived in North America from about 2.5 million to 500,000 years ago and is generally thought to be the ancestor of the larger S. fatalis and S. populator.

A lion-sized early sabre-toothed cat of Late Miocene Eurasia, best known from the fossil-rich pits of Cerro de los Batallones near Madrid, Spain. Its flattened, serrated upper canines were shorter than those of later sabre-tooths such as Smilodon, and its long legs and back gave it a more lion-like build.

One of the largest land mammals of the Ice Age, a ground sloth from South America up to about 6 metres long and weighing several tonnes. It walked on all fours on the outer edges of its feet, with its huge curved claws turned inward, and is thought to have reared up on its hind legs, braced by its thick tail, to pull down branches. Related to today's tree sloths, it died out at the end of the Pleistocene, after people had reached South America.

A giant ground sloth named from Pleistocene fossils found in the Tarija valley of southern Bolivia, in the Andes region. It was smaller than its relative Megatherium americanum of the pampas, but is known from far fewer remains, so its exact size and appearance are less certain.

A three-toed sloth of the rainforests of the Guianas and the northern Amazon basin, told apart from the brown-throated sloth by its pale yellowish throat. It spends almost its whole life hanging from branches by its long hooked claws, eating leaves, and its very slow metabolism suits that low-energy diet. Green algae grow in its shaggy coat, and it climbs down about once a week to defecate at the foot of its tree.

A mostly nocturnal tree sloth of the rainforests of northern South America that hangs upside down in the canopy and feeds on leaves, shoots and fruit. Despite its name it has three toes on each hind foot; only its hands carry two long claws. Two-toed and three-toed sloths are only distantly related and took up their hanging way of life independently.

The oldest known articulated bony fish, about 436 million years old, from early Silurian rocks at Xiushan, Chongqing, China, described in 2026. The near-complete fossil is only about 3 cm long. It already had a bony head and rhombic scales, but also a row of bony plates along its back and spines in front of its fins, features shared with the earliest jawed fishes.

A small jawless, armoured fish (a galeaspid) about 5 cm long, from the early Silurian of Xiushan, Chongqing, China, about 436 million years ago, described in 2022. It lived in shallow coastal seas. Like its relatives it had a broad, flat bony head shield drawn out into horn-like corners, eyes on top of the head and an oval opening on top of the snout. Galeaspids were close relatives of the jawed vertebrates but had no jaws.

The oldest near-complete bony fish found so far, about 425 million years old, from the late Silurian of Qujing, Yunnan, China, described in 2009. About 33 cm long, it combined a skull like that of early lobe-finned fishes with large spines in front of its fins and bony plates behind its head, features otherwise seen in placoderms. Its body was covered in thick rhombic scales.

An early bony fish near the base of the lobe-finned fishes, from the late Silurian and Early Devonian (about 418-397 million years ago) of Qujing, Yunnan, China. It is known mainly from skulls, jaws, shoulder girdles and scales. It had a humped snout, a head coated in shiny, pore-covered cosmine, and large spines in front of its pectoral and dorsal fins, features otherwise seen in early jawed fishes.

One of the earliest known ray-finned fishes, about 420 million years old, from the late Silurian of Gotland, Sweden, with further finds in Estonia, Latvia and Arctic Russia. It is known only from small rhombic scales with a shiny enamel-like coat and a few bone fragments, so its size and body shape are reconstructed from later relatives.

The earliest known tetrapodomorph, a lobe-finned fish from the lineage that later gave rise to four-legged animals, about 409 million years old, from the Early Devonian of Zhaotong, Yunnan, China, described in 2012. It is known from parts of the skull and lower jaw, which had unusually large notches for the eyes. It was a small predator, under about 20 cm long.

The largest bony fish known, a pachycormid of Middle to Late Jurassic seas, first found in the Oxford Clay of England in rocks about 165 million years old. Growth rings in its bones suggest adults of roughly 8-16.5 metres that took decades to reach full size. Its skeleton was largely cartilage, so the fossils are fragmentary, but its huge sieve of gill rakers shows it strained plankton from the water, much like a basking shark.

A filter-feeding pachycormid fish from the Late Cretaceous chalk sea of southern England, about 95 million years ago. Described in 2010 from a single toothless skull, it had extremely long jaw-supporting bones that swung its mouth open into an enormous gape for straining plankton. Only the skull is known; related species from Colorado and Japan suggest bodies roughly 2-4.5 metres long.

A tiny, eel-like vertebrate about 5 cm long, known from thousands of skeletons in the Middle Devonian lake beds of Achanarras, Scotland, about 390 million years ago. Only its cartilage skeleton survives, with no teeth or scales: a small skull with a ring of stiff cirri at the snout, a column of ring-shaped vertebrae and a fin-fringed tail. What kind of fish it was has been debated for more than a century.

An older relative of the Scottish Palaeospondylus, described in 2025 from Early Devonian limestone about 400 million years old in western Queensland, Australia, laid down in a shallow sea. Its tiny braincase is preserved uncrushed in three dimensions, showing details of the brain cavity and inner ear, and it is the smallest fossil vertebrate yet described from Queensland. No complete skeleton is known, so its body is reconstructed after its Scottish cousin.

A small Carboniferous shark known only from tiny three-cusped teeth, first described in 1933 from marine rocks about 320 million years old in Oklahoma, USA, and at first mistaken for a conodont. It belongs to the Bransonelliformes, early relatives of the eel-like xenacanth sharks, and its teeth suggest a body well under a metre long. Its body is reconstructed here after xenacanths, with a long, low dorsal fin and a tapering tail.

A boat-shaped Ediacaran organism from the very end of the period, best known from the Nama Group of Namibia and also found in Russia's White Sea region. Its body had three vanes joined along a central seam, each quilted into rows of narrow tube-like units. It lived partly buried in sand rather than standing up like a frond, and some sandstone beds hold thousands of them packed together. How it fed is uncertain; absorbing nutrients from the water is one idea.

A spindle-shaped rangeomorph that lay flat on the deep seafloor at Mistaken Point, Newfoundland, about 565 million years ago. Its two rows of frondlets branched again and again into smaller copies of themselves. Maps of whole bedding surfaces show that it spread in clusters, probably both by runner-like stolons and by drifting propagules, making it one of the earliest records of how a population of large organisms grew. It is named after S. B. Misra, who found the Mistaken Point fossils in 1967.

A tubular organism from the Ediacara Member of South Australia, about 555 to 550 million years old, whose tubes grew up to 30 cm long and about 1 cm wide, divided along their length into short serial units. It lived in dense patches, sometimes more than a thousand tubes per square metre. Tubes in a cluster are all much the same size, which suggests they settled at the same time, as after a mass spawning; this is among the earliest evidence of sexual reproduction in animals. It may have been a sponge or a relative of cnidarians.

A small, thimble-shaped animal from the Ediacara Member of South Australia, about 555 million years old, up to about 2 cm across and 1.5 cm high. At least four long, straight, needle-like spicules, up to 37 cm long, radiated from its body down to the seafloor and probably propped it up. Described in 2012, it is one of the oldest animals known with hard skeletal parts, and may have been an early sponge.

A small, round, umbrella-shaped Ediacaran organism, about 1 to 4 cm across, with eight arms spiralling out from a central knob. It is unusual in being found both in the Doushantuo Formation of South China and in the Ediacara Member of South Australia. The ridges crossing its arms recall the comb rows of comb jellies, its most likely relatives, and recent work suggests it lived on the seafloor rather than drifting.

A frond from the Ediacara Member of South Australia, about 555 million years old, and among the commonest fronds there. A leaf-shaped blade of many side-by-side primary branches sat on a long, bare, cylindrical stalk anchored in the sand by a bulbous holdfast. It was long confused with Charniodiscus, but differs in its longer stem and bulbous holdfast. Its relationships are uncertain; it may have been an early animal near the base of the cnidarians and their relatives.

The commonest animal of the Burgess Shale of British Columbia, about 508 million years old, known from tens of thousands of specimens and the first fossil Charles Walcott collected there in 1909. Under 2 cm long, it had a small head shield with two pairs of long spines sweeping back over its body, a pair of long antennae and a pair of bristly swimming antennae. Its 26 body segments each bore a leg and a feathery gill branch, and it probably swam just above the mud picking up food particles.

A slug-like Burgess Shale animal up to about 5 cm long, covered in rows of overlapping, ribbed scales with two rows of tall, blade-like spines along its back. It crawled on a soft sole and scraped the microbial film on the mud with a toothed feeding apparatus much like a mollusc's radula. Its relatives have been argued over for decades, but most researchers now see it as an early mollusc or a close relative.

A burrowing priapulid worm from the Burgess Shale, usually about 8 cm long and one of the commonest animals there. It turned its spiny proboscis inside out to seize prey, and its preserved guts often hold the shells of hyoliths, other small animals and sometimes other Ottoia. It probably lived in a U-shaped burrow in the mud, like the living penis worms it is related to.

A broad, flattened arthropod up to about 16 cm long from the Burgess Shale, one of the larger predators of the seafloor there. The spiny bases of its legs could crush shells, and its guts contain the remains of small trilobites, hyoliths and other shelled animals. Walcott named it in 1911 after his son Sidney, who helped find the first specimens.

A shrimp-like Burgess Shale arthropod up to about 8 cm long, with a two-valved carapace over its front half, stalked eyes, long antennae and a slender segmented abdomen ending in two paddle-like tail flaps. Some females carry clusters of eggs under the carapace, the oldest direct evidence of brood care in the fossil record. It probably swam and hunted small soft-bodied prey near the seafloor; it is named after Mount Wapta near the quarry.

A slender Burgess Shale arthropod about 5 cm long, with a downturned snout and a pair of great appendages under its head, each branching into three long, whip-like flagella. It probably used them to feel for and grab small prey as it swam or walked over the mud. It belongs to the megacheirans, early great-appendage arthropods that may be related to the ancestors of spiders and their kin.

The commonest radiodont of the Chengjiang biota of Yunnan, China, about 518 million years old, and a close relative of Anomalocaris. Each frontal appendage carried one enormous forward spine that closed against the rest of the limb like the jaw of a pair of pincers. It swam with eleven pairs of body flaps and had a long tail fan with streamers; a 2023 study of its growth suggests the biggest individuals were well over half a metre long.

A flat, round, jellyfish-like animal from the Burgess Shale, typically several centimetres across, with a coiled gut sac showing through its disc and a tuft of branched feeding tentacles near the mouth. Walcott took it for a swimming sea cucumber. Today eldonids are thought to be early relatives of echinoderms and hemichordates, and they may have rested on the seafloor or drifted, feeding with their tentacles.

A two-part animal about 9 cm long from the Chengjiang biota of Yunnan, China. Its boxy front section of stiff plates had a wide mouth and a row of five gill openings along each side, and behind it a narrower, segmented tail did the swimming. The gill openings suggest vetulicolians were early deuterostomes, the group that includes chordates and echinoderms, though exactly where they belong is still debated.

One of the earliest vertebrates, a small jawless fish about 6 cm long from the Burgess Shale and the nearby Marble Canyon site of British Columbia. It had a pair of large camera eyes, zig-zag muscle blocks along its body and seven pairs of gill bars. The first pair of bars was a little thicker than the rest, foreshadowing the gill arch that later became jaws. Specimens from Marble Canyon were described in 2014.

A spiny trilobite up to about 9 cm long from the Burgess Shale, famous because some fossils keep its legs, antennae and a pair of antenna-like cerci at the tail. Its legs had spiny bases for tearing apart food, so it was probably a predator and scavenger on the seafloor. Some specimens show healed injuries, evidence that it survived attacks by predators.

A gilled lobopodian from the Sirius Passet biota of North Greenland, about 518 million years old and about 17 cm long. It swam with eleven pairs of broad body flaps, carried a pair of long spiny frontal appendages for catching prey and trailed two long tail spines. Small stubby legs under the flaps show it was a link between soft-legged lobopodians and radiodonts such as Anomalocaris; its name honours the philosopher Søren Kierkegaard.

A caterpillar-like lobopodian from the Burgess Shale, a few centimetres long, with ten pairs of stubby, clawed legs and a pair of spiny grasping appendages beside its mouth. It is often found with sponges, and probably clung to them with its claws and fed on their soft tissue. It looks much like a velvet worm, but is now thought to be closer to the stem of the arthropods.

A bristle worm from the Burgess Shale, up to about 5 cm long, with about two dozen segments, each bearing a pair of fleshy parapodia with fans of long bristles. A pair of long tentacles on its head probably gathered food particles from the mud. It is one of the oldest well-preserved polychaete worms.

A sea scorpion from the Late Ordovician (Katian) of southwestern Ohio, about 450 million years ago, roughly 50-80 cm long. Its front legs were long and armed with pairs of very long, movable spines, forming a cage for trapping prey, while its hind legs were broad swimming paddles. Its tail ended in a spine flanked by a pair of serrated blades, which it may have used as a weapon or to steer.

The oldest well-described sea scorpion, from the Middle Ordovician (Darriwilian) Winneshiek Shale of Iowa, about 467 million years ago. Estimated at up to 1.7 m long, it was one of the largest predators of its time. Its name recalls the penteconter, a Greek warship. Like other megalograptids it caught prey with long, spiny front legs and swam with paddle-shaped hind legs; it lived in a brackish coastal inlet.

A giant radiodont from the Early Ordovician Fezouata Biota of Morocco, about 480 million years ago. At around 2 m long it was one of the largest animals of its day, yet it fed on plankton, sieving the water with frontal appendages fringed with fine comb-like spines, like a baleen whale. Each body segment carried two pairs of swimming flaps, upper and lower, which suggests that the two-branched legs of arthropods arose from these two sets of flaps. A long, blade-like plate jutted forward from the top of its head.

A trilobite from the Middle Ordovician limestones near St Petersburg, Russia, about 10 cm long. Its compound eyes sat on top of extraordinarily long, thin stalks rising straight up from its head. It probably lay buried in the sediment with only its eyes above the sea floor, watching for predators such as nautiloids. Beautifully preserved specimens from the region are prized by collectors.

A small blind trilobite from the Early Ordovician Fezouata Shale of Morocco, with a body under 2 cm long. A long spine projected forward from its head and two more swept back from its cheeks. Fossils show groups of Ampyx lined up in single file, each touching the one in front with its spines: probably a collective migration, perhaps triggered by storms, and among the oldest evidence of group behaviour in animals.

A flat, spiny odontopleurid trilobite from the Middle and Late Ordovician of Bohemia and Morocco, around 10 cm long. Every segment of its thorax ended in a long, slender spine curving backwards, and long spines also trailed from its cheeks and tail, making it about as wide as it was long. The spines may have deterred predators and helped spread its weight on soft mud.

A spiny cheirurid trilobite from the Middle to Late Ordovician of New York and Ontario, usually a few centimetres long. It had a bulbous, furrowed glabella, long backward-curving cheek spines, short spiny segment tips and two long spines on its small tail. Specimens from the Walcott-Rust Quarry in New York preserve its legs and gills, showing how trilobite limbs were built. It probably hunted or scavenged small animals on the sea floor.

One of the most common trilobites of the Late Ordovician seas around Cincinnati, Ohio, typically 3-5 cm long. Its strongly arched shell had a bell-shaped, lobed glabella, small eyes and a thorax of thirteen segments, with no spines. It is very often found rolled up into a tight ball, a defence that protected its soft underside from predators and from smothering mud.

A jawless armoured fish from the Middle Ordovician of Bolivia, about 465 million years ago, around 25-35 cm long. Its head was encased in large bony shields, and its tiny eyes sat at the very front of the head, facing forward like a car's headlights. It had no paired fins and probably swam clumsily near the bottom of shallow coastal seas, sucking in small food particles through a small, jawless mouth.

One of the oldest known vertebrates with a bony armour, from the Early to Middle Ordovician Stairway Sandstone of central Australia. About 15 cm long, it had flattened dorsal and ventral head shields joined by rows of small plates over the gills, tiny eyes at the front of the head, no paired fins and no jaws. Its body was covered in long, narrow, saw-edged scales, which gave it its name.

A jawless armoured fish from the Late Ordovician Harding Sandstone of Colorado, about 450 million years ago. Its head armour was a mosaic of small bony plates, each capped with shiny star-shaped tubercles (its name means 'star shield'), and it had eyes on the sides of its head and eight separate gill openings on each side. About 13-15 cm long, it lived in shallow coastal waters and is one of the earliest vertebrates known from reasonably complete fossils.

A giant conodont from the latest Ordovician (Hirnantian) Soom Shale of South Africa, about 444 million years ago, estimated at around 40 cm long. Conodonts were eel-like early vertebrates known mostly from their tiny tooth-like elements; Promissum fossils also preserve the muscles of its large eyes and its V-shaped trunk muscle blocks. It lived in cold water during the end-Ordovician ice age and probably grasped and sliced prey with its complex feeding apparatus.

A Middle Ordovician nautiloid from Sweden and the Baltic region, with a shell shaped like a bishop's crook: a small coil of a few whorls at the start, followed by a long straight tube up to about 30 cm long. The opening of the shell had two ear-like side flaps. The animal probably drifted slowly near the sea floor, catching small prey with its tentacles, and the striking shells are common in Swedish Orthoceras limestones.

A cystoid echinoderm from the Middle Ordovician of the Baltic region: a ball of thin calcite plates 2-4 cm across, with a small mouth on top surrounded by a few short arm-like brachioles. Slits called pore rhombs crossed its plate sutures and probably helped it breathe. Young ones were attached by a short stem, but adults lay loose on the sea floor, and they were so abundant that their globes form whole beds of 'Echinosphaerites limestone'.

A small sea lily from the Late Ordovician (Katian) of the Cincinnati region. Its small cup was held above the sea floor on a long, ridged stem anchored by a root-like holdfast, and its five arms branched repeatedly into a fan that caught food particles drifting in the current. Whole crinoids like it are sometimes found tangled together in 'logjams', smothered by storm-stirred mud.

One of the earliest true starfish, from the Late Ordovician (Katian) of the Cincinnati region, a few centimetres across. Its small disc and five short, broad arms were built of neat rows of block-like plates, with large plates along the edges of each arm. Early starfish like it crept over the sea floor on tube feet and probably fed on small animals and organic debris.

A small sea snail, about 2 cm high, very common in Late Ordovician rocks of Ohio, Indiana and Kentucky. Its top-shaped shell had a few rounded whorls and a large round opening, and was covered in fine spiral ridges crossed by growth lines. It probably crept over the sea floor grazing on microbial films and organic debris.

A large, thick-shelled brachiopod from the Late Ordovician of the Cincinnati region, a few centimetres wide. Its strongly swollen valves had a straight hinge, a few coarse, sharp ribs on each side, and a high fold in one valve fitting a deep groove in the other, so the shell margin zig-zagged where the two met. It lay on the sea floor filtering food from the water with a coiled feeding organ inside the shell, and is one of the most common fossils of the region.

A colonial 'moss animal' from the Late Ordovician seas of eastern North America. Each colony was a hemispherical, gumdrop-like mound of calcite a few centimetres across, flat underneath, made of thousands of tiny tubes, each housing a zooid that filtered food with a crown of tentacles; the surface was dotted with small bumps called monticules. Bryozoans diversified explosively during the Ordovician and became important builders of sea-floor communities.

A planktonic graptolite of the Early Ordovician, about 477 million years ago, whose colony of four slender, horizontal branches spread out from a tiny founding tube in two close pairs. Each branch carried a row of small cups, each holding a filter-feeding zooid. It spread across the world's oceans so quickly that its first appearance is used to define the start of the Floian Stage of the Ordovician.

The oldest known horseshoe crab, from Late Ordovician shallow-marine rocks in Manitoba, Canada, about 445 million years ago. It was only about 4 cm long, with a large crescent-shaped head shield bearing small eyes, a segmented abdomen and a long, spear-like tail spine. Its body plan already resembled that of living horseshoe crabs, which have changed remarkably little since.

The best-known sea scorpion, from the Late Silurian of New York and Ontario, about 420 million years ago, and the state fossil of New York. Most individuals were 10-20 cm long. It swam with a pair of broad, paddle-shaped hind legs, caught small prey with its spiny front legs and had a long, slender, spike-like tail. Thousands of specimens are known from the shallow, salty lagoons of the Bertie Group.

A giant pterygotid sea scorpion from the Late Silurian of New York and Ontario, about 420 million years ago; tergites 45 cm wide show it grew to more than 2 metres long. It held a pair of huge pincers forward, their long rami lined with sharp, inclined teeth, and it steered with a flat, spear-shaped tail. Its name means 'large eye', for the big compound eyes on the front corners of its head. It was among the largest predators of its time.

A large sea scorpion, up to about a metre long, from the Silurian of Lesmahagow in southern Scotland, about 430 million years ago. It had a long, rectangular head shield with small eyes at its front corners, slender spiny walking legs and swimming paddles. Its long, flattened tail ended in a serrated, blade-like telson that may have worked as a rudder or a weapon. It probably hunted small animals and jawless fish on the sea floor.

A sea scorpion about 75 cm long from the Late Silurian of Ringerike, Norway, about 420 million years ago. Its first two pairs of walking legs were long and armed with long paired spines, forming a basket to trap prey. It may have carried its narrow, spike-tipped tail arched over its back like a scorpion. It lived in shallow coastal and brackish water.

One of the earliest scorpions, about 4 cm long, from the Late Silurian Bertie Group of New York, about 420 million years ago. It already had the scorpion body plan: grasping pincers, four pairs of walking legs and a curled tail ending in a sting. It lacks clear evidence of book lungs, so it probably still lived in shallow water or at its edges rather than fully on land.

A tiny chelicerate about 5 mm long from the Herefordshire Lagerstaette of England, about 430 million years ago, preserved in three dimensions in volcanic ash. Its broad, horseshoe-shaped head shield covered a ring of legs, some carrying fringed outer branches, and its short body ended in a spine-like tail. It is an early relative of horseshoe crabs and sea scorpions.

The oldest well-preserved sea spider, from the Herefordshire Lagerstaette of England, about 430 million years ago; its body was only a few millimetres long. It had four pairs of long, jointed legs on a slender trunk, a long proboscis, a big pair of claws at the front and, unlike living sea spiders, a long segmented tail. Like its living relatives it probably fed on soft-bodied animals such as sponges and hydroids.

A tiny trigonotarbid, a few millimetres long, from the Late Silurian of Ludford Lane in Shropshire, England, about 420 million years ago, and the oldest known arachnid that lived on land. Trigonotarbids looked like spiders with armoured, segmented bodies but had no silk glands or venom. It hunted even smaller arthropods among the first low land plants.

A small, millipede-like myriapod from the island of Kerrera in western Scotland, dated to about 425 million years ago, which makes it one of the oldest known land animals. Its slender body was made of simple, rounded segments, each bearing a pair of legs on each side. It lived around a lake among early plants and probably fed on decaying plant matter and microbial mats.

A small anaspid, a jawless fish about 10 cm long, from the Silurian of Lesmahagow and the Hagshaw Hills in southern Scotland, about 430 million years ago. Its deep body was covered in rows of narrow scales, with a crest of hooked scales along its back and a row of small gill openings behind each eye. Its tail bent down into a large lower lobe. It probably fed on small food particles near the sea floor.

A slender, eel-like jawless fish about 17 cm long from the early Silurian of Lesmahagow, Scotland, about 430 million years ago. Its body was soft and only lightly scaled, with a long fin fold along each side, a round mouth, large eyes and a row of gill openings. It may be a relative of the anaspids or of the lampreys, and it probably sucked up small food from the water or the sea floor.

A thelodont, a jawless fish about 12 cm long, known from complete specimens from the Silurian of Lesmahagow, Scotland. Thelodonts were covered in thousands of tiny, tooth-like scales rather than bony plates. It had a broad, flattened head with flap-like pectoral fins and a deeply forked tail, and probably fed on small particles on or near the sea floor. Thelodont scales are some of the most common vertebrate fossils of the Silurian.

An armoured placoderm about 20 cm long from the Late Silurian Kuanti Formation of Qujing, Yunnan, China, about 423 million years ago, described in 2013. Its head and trunk were boxed in bony plates like other placoderms, but its mouth was edged with the same jaw bones (maxilla and dentary) found in bony fishes, including ourselves. Its name means 'complete jaw'. It showed that the bony fish jaw first evolved in placoderms.

An armoured placoderm about 20 cm long from the Late Silurian Kuanti Formation of Qujing, Yunnan, China, about 423 million years ago, described in 2016. Like Entelognathus it combined a box-like placoderm armour with bony-fish-like jaw bones, but its snout was drawn out into a short, pointed rostrum. It was named after the qilin, a chimera of Chinese mythology, because it mixes features of different fish groups.

A large lobe-finned fish from the Late Silurian Kuanti Formation of Qujing, Yunnan, China, about 423 million years ago, estimated at about a metre long. It is known only from big lower jaws and a jaw bone armed with blunt, crushing teeth, so its body is reconstructed after its relative Guiyu. Its name means 'big mouth', and it was probably the largest vertebrate of its time, preying on armoured fishes.

A trilobite about 6 cm long from the Wenlock Limestone of Dudley, England, about 428 million years ago, so common there that it was nicknamed the 'Dudley Bug' and appears on the town's coat of arms. It had a tall, lobed glabella, small eyes, thirteen body segments and a small tail shield, and it could roll up into a tight ball for protection. It fed on organic debris on the floors of shallow reef seas.

A phacopid trilobite about 6 cm long from the mid-Silurian Rochester Shale of New York, about 428 million years ago. It had long genal spines, a tail shield ending in a long spine, and large, tall compound eyes made of separate lenses, each with its own cornea. It probably hunted or scavenged small animals on the muddy sea floor.

A trilobite about 5 cm long from the mid-Silurian Wenlock Limestone of England and the reefs of Gotland, about 428 million years ago. Its head was covered in coarse tubercles, giving it the nickname 'strawberry-headed trilobite', and its small eyes were raised on short stalks. It had a long, triangular tail shield with many rings and lived on the floors of shallow reef seas.

A large, smooth, oval brachiopod up to about 10 cm long from the early Silurian (Llandovery), about 435 million years ago. It formed dense shell banks across Britain, the Baltic and North America, the shells packed so tightly that they stood upright with their beaks sunk in the mud. Inside, a deep spoon-shaped plate supported by a septum held the muscles, which shows as a line on worn shells.

A sea lily (crinoid) from the mid-Silurian reefs of Gotland, Sweden, and the Wenlock Limestone of England, about 428 million years ago. A stout stem anchored by roots held up a small cup whose many-branched arms were joined side by side into five broad, net-like fans. Spread out, the fans formed a wide funnel that strained food from the current; folded together they looked like a rattle, which gives the genus its name.

A lobe-finned fish from the Late Devonian estuary of Miguasha in Quebec, about 380 million years ago, and one of the best-studied fossil fishes. It grew up to about 1.8 metres long and was a fast ambush hunter with a torpedo-shaped body and a distinctive three-lobed tail. The bones inside its fleshy pectoral and pelvic fins follow the same one-bone, two-bone pattern as the arms and legs of four-limbed animals.

A lobe-finned fish from the Late Devonian of Latvia and Estonia, about 380 million years ago, among the closest fish relatives of four-limbed animals. About a metre long, it had a broad, flat, crocodile-like head with eyes on top, no dorsal or anal fins and only a low fin around its tail tip. It probably lurked in shallow coastal waters and deltas, and the bones of its pectoral fin already show the beginnings of digits.

A giant tristichopterid lobe-finned fish from the Late Devonian rivers of Pennsylvania, about 365 million years ago, estimated at 2.5 to 3 metres long. It had a broad, blunt head armed with large fangs, small eyes and a well-developed sensory-canal system that may have let it hunt in murky water. As the largest predator of the Red Hill site, it may even have eaten early tetrapods.

A large porolepiform lobe-finned fish from the Late Devonian Old Red Sandstone of Scotland; its genus was widespread in rivers around the world, about 380 to 360 million years ago. It had a deep body covered in big, thick, rounded scales with wavy ridges, long pointed pectoral fins, fangs, and dorsal and anal fins set far back next to the tail. Some Holoptychius grew well over a metre long and were major predators of their river systems.

One of the earliest well-known ray-finned fishes, the group that now includes almost all living fish, from the Middle Devonian lakes of northern Scotland about 385 million years ago. Usually 25 to 55 centimetres long, it had large eyes, long toothed jaws and tiny diamond-shaped scales. It could swallow prey up to a third of its own length, including other fishes.

One of the earliest lungfishes, from the Middle Devonian lakes of the Orcadian Basin in Scotland, about 385 million years ago. About 35 centimetres long, it had two dorsal fins, long leaf-shaped paired fins and broad tooth plates for crushing shellfish and other hard-shelled prey. Like modern lungfish it could probably gulp air when the water became warm and stale.

One of the earliest well-known sharks, from the Late Devonian Cleveland Shale of Ohio, about 370 million years ago, reaching up to about 1.8 metres. It had a streamlined body with a crescent-shaped tail, big triangular pectoral fins, spined dorsal fins and a mouth at the very front of the snout. Its skin was almost free of scales, and fossil stomach contents show it swallowed fishes and shrimp tail-first after chasing them down.

A small armoured placoderm from the Middle Devonian lakes of northern Scotland, about 385 million years ago, and a smaller, earlier relative of Dunkleosteus. About 40 centimetres long, it had a jointed head-and-thorax shield covered in tubercles, sharp bony jaw plates instead of teeth, and a naked, tapering tail. Its neck joint let it lift its head and open its jaws very wide to swallow other fish.

A small ptyctodont placoderm from the Late Devonian Gogo reef of Western Australia, about 380 million years ago, named in honour of David Attenborough. Its fossil, the 'mother fish', contains an embryo still joined to it by an umbilical cord, the oldest known evidence of live birth in any vertebrate. About 25 centimetres long, it had big eyes, beak-like crushing tooth plates for shellfish and a long, whip-like tail.

An antiarch placoderm from the Late Devonian Miguasha estuary of Quebec, about 380 million years ago; its genus is the most widespread placoderm, found on every continent. About 30 to 40 centimetres long, its front half was a box of bony plates with the eyes together on top, and jointed, armour-plated arm-like pectoral fins. It probably grubbed through the mud for food, perhaps using its arms to prop itself up or push along the bottom.

A jawless armoured fish (a heterostracan) from the Early Devonian of Britain and western Europe, about 415 million years ago. About 20 centimetres long, its front half was enclosed in a streamlined bony shield with a long pointed snout, a dorsal spine and two wing-like side spines that may have kept it stable while swimming. Having no jaws, it probably fed on small particles and plankton in coastal waters and estuaries.

A very flat, broad jawless fish (a heterostracan) from the Early Devonian Hunsrück Slate of Germany, about 400 million years ago. About 35 centimetres long, its plate-like head shield was made of a few large plates set in a mosaic of small bony tiles, with tiny eyes far apart at the front corners. Its jawless mouth opened upward at the front edge, and it probably lay on the muddy sea floor feeding on organic debris.

A jawless armoured fish (an osteostracan) from the Early Devonian Old Red Sandstone of Scotland, about 415 million years ago, named after the geologist Charles Lyell. It had a flat, horseshoe-shaped head shield with backward-pointing horns, eyes close together on top and patches of sensory 'fields' along its edges. Osteostracans were the first fishes with paired pectoral fins, and Cephalaspis probably fed on the bottom of rivers and lakes through a small mouth underneath.

A ray-like placoderm from the Early Devonian Hunsrück Slate of Germany, about 400 million years ago, about 25 to 30 centimetres long. With its flat body, broad wing-like pectoral fins, upward-looking eyes and long thin tail, it looked remarkably like a modern skate, a striking case of convergent evolution. Its skin was covered in small bony tiles, and it probably lay on the sea floor and fed on small invertebrates.

One of the earliest four-limbed vertebrates, from the Late Devonian of East Greenland about 365 million years ago, about 60 centimetres long. It had legs with eight digits on each foot, but they were paddle-like and too weak to carry it far on land, and it still had internal gills and a deep tail fin. It lived mostly in shallow, weedy river channels, showing that limbs with digits first evolved in the water.

A classic phacopid trilobite from the Middle Devonian seas of Germany, Morocco and South America, about 390 million years ago, usually 4 to 6 centimetres long. Its large eyes had dozens of separate calcite lenses each, and a big, bumpy glabella swelled out over the front of its head. It is often found rolled up tightly into a ball, like a pill-bug, for protection.

A spiny trilobite from the Early Devonian of Morocco, about 400 million years ago, famous for the long three-pronged 'trident' sticking out from the front of its head. Besides the trident it carried long cheek spines, a spine on every body segment and spikes above its large eyes. The trident may have been used by males in contests, like the horns of a stag beetle.

One of the early goniatites, ammonoids from the Middle Devonian seas of New York, Europe and North Africa, about 390 million years ago. Its smooth, flattened shell, about 10 to 15 centimetres across, was loosely coiled with a wide central hollow and carried fine, strongly curved growth lines. Ammonoids first appeared in the Devonian, and like their later relatives they used gas-filled chambers to float while hunting small prey.

A trigonotarbid, an extinct spider-like arachnid, from the Early Devonian Rhynie chert of Scotland, about 410 million years ago and only a few millimetres long. It had no silk glands or venom, but was one of the first predators on land, hunting other tiny arthropods among the early plants around hot springs. The chert preserves it in such detail that its book lungs can be seen, showing it breathed air.

A close relative of true spiders from the Middle Devonian of Gilboa, New York, about 386 million years ago, only a few millimetres long. It could already produce silk from rows of spigots on its abdomen, but lacked true spinnerets, so it probably used silk to line burrows or wrap eggs rather than to spin webs. Unlike spiders it kept a segmented abdomen and a long, whip-like tail.

One of the oldest known centipedes, from the Middle Devonian of Gilboa, New York, about 386 million years ago, and around a centimetre long. It already had a pair of venom claws under its head, long antennae and a flat body with a pair of legs on each segment. It hunted small arthropods in the leaf litter of some of the earliest forests, and is the only member of its own extinct order, Devonobiomorpha.

A springtail from the Early Devonian Rhynie chert of Scotland, about 410 million years ago, and one of the oldest six-legged animals known. Only 1 to 2 millimetres long, it had short antennae, three pairs of legs and a forked jumping organ folded under its abdomen that could fling it into the air. It lived in the damp plant litter around hot springs, feeding on fungi, algae and decaying plants.

The earliest known diapsid reptile, the lineage that later gave rise to lizards, crocodiles and dinosaurs, from Late Carboniferous rocks near Garnett, Kansas, about 302 million years old. It was a slender animal some 40 cm long, with a small head, a long neck, long legs and a tail longer than the rest of its body. It probably darted through the undergrowth of the coal forests hunting insects and other small invertebrates.

One of the oldest known synapsids, the group that much later produced mammals, found in fossilised tree stumps at Florence, Nova Scotia, about 306 million years old. It looked like a lizard about half a metre long, but its skull already had the single opening behind each eye typical of synapsids. Its sharp teeth, including enlarged ones near the front of the upper jaw, suggest it hunted insects and small tetrapods in the coal forests.

A small, long-bodied tetrapod about 20 cm long from East Kirkton in Scotland, about 338 million years old, where it lived around a volcanic lake together with early scorpions and amphibians. Nicknamed 'Lizzie', it was first hailed as the oldest reptile, but it is now seen as a close relative of the amniotes rather than a true reptile. It had a long trunk, short little limbs and a long tail, and probably hunted small invertebrates among the plants.

A fully aquatic early tetrapod about 2 metres long from Early Carboniferous coal-swamp rocks of Scotland, around 330 million years old. It had a huge, deep skull with jaws that opened very wide and big fangs, large eyes, a long eel-like body and absurdly tiny forelimbs that were useless on land. It probably lurked in swamp lakes and ambushed fish with a sudden lunge and a powerful bite.

An early tetrapod about a metre long from Dumbarton in Scotland, about 348 million years old, one of the few known from 'Romer's Gap', the poorly fossilised start of the Carboniferous. It had a broad, triangular head, a stout body and sturdy limbs, and its feet are the oldest known to point forward, a sign that it walked on land rather than only paddling. It probably hunted along the edges of rivers and swamps.

An early embolomere from Early Carboniferous rocks of West Virginia, about 325 million years old, and one of the best known of these long-bodied relatives of the amniotes. It reached about 1.5 metres, with a deep, crocodile-like skull lined with sharp teeth, well-formed legs and a long, tall, flattened tail. It probably lived much like a small crocodile, hunting fish and smaller tetrapods in and around swamp waters.

A small temnospondyl amphibian about 12 cm long from the Mazon Creek fossil beds of Illinois, about 309 million years old. It had a broad, rounded head with huge eye sockets, a short body and slender legs, and its fossils include larvae with gills, so it grew up in the water like a salamander. Amphibamus is one of the closest known Palaeozoic relatives of modern frogs and salamanders, and probably snapped up insects and other small invertebrates.

A stethacanthid shark about 65 cm long from Bearsden near Glasgow in Scotland, about 330 million years old, known from exceptionally complete fossils. Its strangest feature was a tall dorsal spine topped by a flat, anvil-shaped 'brush' whose upper surface, like the top of its head, was covered with enlarged tooth-like denticles. The brush may have been a display structure or helped to make the shark look too big to swallow; it hunted fish and squid-like animals in shallow seas.

A small shark about 30 cm long from the Bear Gulch Limestone of Montana, laid down in a tropical bay about 320 million years ago. Mature males carried a sword-shaped spine that grew from the shoulders and curved forward over the head, perhaps used in courtship, while females lacked it. With its very large eyes it probably hunted small fish and invertebrates, and some fossils preserve a male with a female apparently gripping his spine.

A giant shark-like eugeneodont fish from the Late Carboniferous seas of North America and Russia, about 310 million years ago; its whorls suggest it grew to more than 6.7 metres long. Almost all that is known of it are curved blades studded with large, serrated triangular teeth that ran along the middle of both its upper and lower jaws. The two blades closed together like a pair of shears, and it may have hunted by slashing through schools of fish.

A small chimaeroid, an early relative of today's ratfish, from the Bear Gulch Limestone of Montana, about 320 million years old. Males grew to about 15 cm and females to only half that, and males bore rows of short spines over the head and back. It had a big blunt head, large eyes, broad pectoral fins and a paddle-like tail, so it was probably a slow swimmer that picked small invertebrates off the bottom of the bay.

The largest known lobe-finned fish, a rhizodont from Early Carboniferous rivers and lagoons of Scotland, about 335 million years ago, estimated at up to about 7 metres long. Its jaws carried enormous fangs, some about 22 cm long, and it had big fleshy pectoral fins. It was the top predator of its waters and could probably catch large fish and even early tetrapods venturing into the shallows.

A sea scorpion about 54 cm long from freshwater rocks of Argentina about 300 million years old, at the very end of the Carboniferous. When it was described in 1980 it was taken for the largest spider that ever lived, but better fossils showed in 2005 that it was a mycteroptid eurypterid. It had a broad, rounded head shield and a wide body, and probably raked through the mud with the spiny front legs, sweeping up small animals.

A small horseshoe crab a few centimetres long, common among the Mazon Creek fossils of Illinois, about 309 million years old. Its broad, crescent-shaped head shield ended in long, backswept spines, and its fused hind shield was fringed with short spines in front of a long tail spike. Unlike today's horseshoe crabs it lived in fresh and brackish coal-swamp waters, and some researchers think it could even clamber about on plants out of the water.

A small whip spider from the Middle Coal Measures of Coseley in England, about 315 million years old, long known as Graeophonus anglicus. Like modern amblypygids it had a flat body and used its enormously long, thin first legs as feelers while walking on the other three pairs. Scans of its fossils show the least specialised pedipalps of any whip spider, still moving up and down like walking legs, which it used to seize insects in the leaf litter of the coal forests.

One of the largest palaeodictyopterans, beaked insects of the coal forests, known from the Mazon Creek beds of Illinois, about 309 million years old. Its wings spanned perhaps 50 to 55 centimetres, rivalling the griffinflies, and like other palaeodictyopterans it could not fold them back over its body. It had a pair of small winglets in front of the wings and a long piercing-sucking beak, probably used to drink sap or suck out the spores and seeds of plants.

A palaeodictyopteran insect from the Late Carboniferous shales of Commentry in France, about 300 million years old, one of the best known members of this extinct order. Like its relatives it had wings on all three thoracic segments: two pairs of long, patterned wings held out flat and a pair of small, lobe-like winglets on the first segment that give the species its name. With its sucking beak it probably fed on plant juices, spores and seeds high in the coal-forest trees.

A puzzling soft-bodied animal up to about 35 cm long, known from thousands of fossils in the Mazon Creek beds of Illinois, about 309 million years old, and now the state fossil of Illinois. It had a segmented, torpedo-shaped body with a tail fin, a long, thin proboscis tipped with a small toothed claw, and its eyes sat at the ends of a stiff bar sticking out sideways from its body. Scientists still disagree on whether it was a vertebrate, a worm-like invertebrate or something else entirely; it probably swam in shallow coastal waters, grabbing small prey with its claw.

A sail-backed plant-eater about 3 metres long from the Early Permian red beds of Texas, around 290 million years ago. Unlike its predatory look-alike Dimetrodon it had a small, short head with blunt, peg-like teeth and tooth plates on the palate for grinding tough plants, set on a broad barrel-shaped body. The tall spines of its sail carried many short sideways crossbars, a feature found in no other sail-back. It was one of the earliest large plant-eating land vertebrates.

A giant caseid synapsid about 4 metres long from the late Early Permian of Oklahoma and Texas, around 275 million years ago. Its enormous barrel-shaped body held a huge gut for fermenting tough plants, while its head was absurdly small, with a short, overhanging snout and large nostrils. Its short, powerful limbs ended in big claws, perhaps used to dig up or pull down plants. It was among the largest land animals of its time.

An early synapsid about 2 metres long from the Early Permian of Texas, around 295 million years ago. Its very long, tall and narrow skull, up to a quarter of its body length, was lined with many sharp teeth. It probably lived along rivers and swamps, catching fish and smaller tetrapods in the water and on the banks. Its family is one of the oldest branches of the synapsid line that later led to mammals.

A slender, monitor-lizard-like hunter about 1.2 metres long from the Early Permian of Texas, around 280 million years ago. It had a narrow skull with sharp, recurved, blade-like teeth, long legs and a long tail, and was more agile than most early synapsids. Despite its lizard-like look it was a synapsid, distantly related to mammals. Bite marks on one Varanops skeleton are among the oldest known evidence of scavenging.

A sturdy tetrapod about 60 cm long from the Early Permian of Texas, named after the town of Seymour. It was so well suited to life on dry land, with strong limbs and a reptile-like skeleton, that it was long thought to be an early reptile. Fossil relatives with gill-bearing, water-living young show it was in fact close to the ancestors of amniotes, still laying eggs in water. It hunted insects, millipedes and other small animals.

A heavily armoured pareiasaur about 2.5 metres long from the Late Permian of European Russia, around 255 million years ago. Its bulky body was studded with bony plates and knobs, and its broad, flat head carried bony bosses and blunt spikes on the cheeks and jaw. It browsed on plants along river floodplains with leaf-shaped, serrated teeth. Its main predator was the giant gorgonopsian Inostrancevia.

One of the largest land-dwelling amphibians of its time, about 2 metres long, from the earliest Permian of Texas and New Mexico. Its huge, broad, flat head, about a quarter of its length, held many sharp teeth and fangs on the palate. It had a sturdy skeleton and strong legs and probably lived much like a crocodile, catching fish and smaller tetrapods in swamps and rivers. It belongs to the temnospondyls, a large group of early amphibians.

An aquatic amphibian about 1 metre long from Early Permian streams and ponds of Texas and Oklahoma, around 285 million years ago. Its flat skull had long, swept-back horns at the corners, giving it a boomerang shape that may have helped it glide through the water like a hydrofoil or made it hard for predators to swallow. Its body was flat, with tiny limbs and a short tail. It probably lay on the bottom and ambushed small prey.

A massive plant-eating dinocephalian about 2.7 metres long from the Middle Permian Karoo of South Africa, around 265 million years ago. It had a short, deep head with a skull roof thickened up to 10 cm of bone, which it may have used in head-butting contests. Its back sloped steeply from high, powerful shoulders to the hips, its forelimbs sprawled while its hind limbs stood more upright, and its chisel-like front teeth cropped tough plants. It probably lived in herds.

A small dicynodont about 45 cm long, one of the most common animals of the Late Permian Karoo of South Africa, around 258 million years ago; it is also known from China. It cropped plants with a horny beak, and many individuals had a pair of small tusks. It dug spiral burrows with its clawed forelimbs, and skeletons have been found curled up inside them, sometimes in pairs. Its name means 'two weasel teeth'.

The namesake of the gorgonopsians, a sabre-toothed predator about 2 metres long from the Late Permian Karoo of South Africa, around 258 million years ago. Its long skull held long, blade-like upper canines and could open in a huge gape to drive them into prey. Its legs were held more upright than in earlier synapsids, making it an agile hunter of dicynodonts and pareiasaurs. Gorgonopsians were the top predators of the Late Permian until they vanished in the end-Permian mass extinction.

One of the first reptiles to return to the water, about 1 metre long, from the Early Permian of Brazil, Uruguay and southern Africa, around 280 million years ago. It swam with its long, deep tail and webbed hind feet, and its long, narrow jaws bristled with long, needle-like teeth for catching or straining small crustaceans. It lived in a vast, shallow, salty inland sea. Finding the same small coastal reptile, which could not have crossed an ocean, in both South America and Africa was early evidence that the two continents were once joined.

One of the earliest gliding vertebrates, a lizard-like reptile about 40 cm long from the Late Permian of Germany, England and Madagascar, around 255 million years ago. It glided between trees on skin wings stretched over long, slender rods of bone that grew from its flanks, a structure unlike that of any living animal. The back of its skull bore a frill of spiky points. It probably hunted insects in the trees.

A large cartilaginous fish, perhaps 5 to 7 metres long, from Early Permian seas around 280 million years ago; its fossils come from the Ural Mountains and from western North America. It is famous for its tooth-whorl, a coiled spiral of well over a hundred serrated teeth set in the middle of the lower jaw. New teeth grew at the outside of the coil while the old ones rolled inward, and closing the jaw sliced and pulled soft prey such as squid-like cephalopods back into the mouth. It was more closely related to ratfishes than to true sharks.

The largest insect known, a griffinfly with a wingspan of about 71 centimetres from the Early Permian of Kansas and Oklahoma, around 275 million years ago. Like its Carboniferous relative Meganeura it was a giant cousin of modern dragonflies, catching other insects in flight with its spiny legs. It had a slightly longer body and narrower wings than Meganeura. Its size may have been possible because the air of the time was richer in oxygen than today.

An ammonoid from the Early Permian seas of west Texas and Mexico, around 280 million years ago. Its smooth, disc-shaped shell, about 10 cm across, was tightly coiled so that each whorl almost hid the one before. The walls between its gas-filled chambers met the shell in very complex, finely frilled suture lines, early examples of the pattern later typical of ammonites. It is a common index fossil of Permian rocks in the Glass Mountains of Texas.

A slender early theropod dinosaur about 3 metres long but weighing only around 20 kg, from the Late Triassic of the south-western United States about 212 million years ago. It had a long, narrow head with many small serrated teeth, a long S-shaped neck, grasping hands and long bird-like legs. Hundreds of skeletons were found together in the Ghost Ranch quarry of New Mexico, and it is New Mexico's state fossil; a Coelophysis skull was even taken to the space station Mir in 1998.

One of the earliest large meat-eating dinosaurs, a biped up to about 6 metres long from the roughly 231-million-year-old Ischigualasto Formation of north-western Argentina. Its long, narrow skull had a flexible joint in the lower jaw to grip struggling prey with big recurved teeth, and its strong arms ended in three-fingered grasping hands. It lived alongside Eoraptor and hunted rhynchosaurs and cynodonts, though it was itself prey for the giant Saurosuchus.

A large early long-necked plant-eater from the Late Triassic of central Europe, about 214 to 204 million years ago, reaching 5 to 10 metres long. It walked on its hind legs, as its hands could not turn palm-down to walk on, and used a large thumb claw for defence or gathering plants, while leaf-shaped teeth shredded vegetation. Its bones are among the most common dinosaur fossils in Europe; dozens of skeletons, mired in mud, are known from Trossingen in Germany and Frick in Switzerland. Growth rings show that individuals of the same age could differ greatly in size, depending on their surroundings.

A crocodile-line archosaur about 2-3 metres long from the Late Triassic Ghost Ranch quarry of New Mexico, about 210 million years ago, named after the painter Georgia O'Keeffe who lived nearby. Although more closely related to crocodiles than to dinosaurs, it looked astonishingly like the much later ostrich dinosaurs: a toothless beaked head with big eyes on a long neck, tiny arms, and long legs on which it walked upright. It is a striking case of convergent evolution, and was found in blocks of rock collected decades before it was recognised in 2006.

A giant four-legged crocodile-line predator, 6 to 7 metres long, from the roughly 231-million-year-old Ischigualasto Formation of Argentina. Its legs were held erect under its body rather than sprawling, and its huge, deep skull was armed with long serrated teeth; two rows of bony scutes ran down its back. It was the top predator of its ecosystem, larger than the early dinosaurs it lived with, such as Herrerasaurus and Eoraptor.

A heavily armoured, plant-eating crocodile-line archosaur about 4.5 metres long from the Late Triassic of Texas, New Mexico and Arizona, about 220 to 205 million years ago. Its broad, low body was covered in interlocking rows of bony plates, and a pair of long, curved spikes jutted from its shoulders to fend off predators. The small head ended in a blunt, shovel-like snout, probably used to root up plants and grubs.

A stocky, barrel-bodied rhynchosaur about 1.3 metres long from the Late Triassic Lossiemouth Sandstone near Elgin in Scotland, about 230 million years ago. Its broad, triangular skull ended in a hooked beak, and rows of teeth on its upper jaw fitted into a groove in the lower jaw to slice tough seed-ferns like secateurs. Rhynchosaurs of its genus were so abundant worldwide, from Brazil and Argentina to India, that they make up most of the fossils in some rock layers, and they are used to match Late Triassic rocks across continents.

One of the last and largest dicynodonts, a hippo-like plant-eater about 3.5 metres long and weighing up to a tonne, from the Late Triassic of Arizona about 220 million years ago. It cropped plants with a toothless horny beak and had a pair of short tusks growing from bony bosses on its upper jaw. The remains of about 40 individuals were found together in the Placerias Quarry near St. Johns, Arizona, suggesting it lived in herds.

A small, fox-sized cynodont, about 45 cm long, from the Early Triassic of South Africa and Antarctica, around 250 million years ago, soon after the end-Permian mass extinction. Its teeth were already divided into incisors, canines and cheek teeth, and its ribcage hints that it breathed with a diaphragm, like mammals. Many fossils were found curled up in burrows, one of which it shared with an injured amphibian, suggesting it sheltered underground from the harsh climate.

One of the oldest turtles with a complete shell, about 1 metre long, from the Late Triassic of Germany about 210 million years ago. Its high, domed shell was edged with spiky plates, but it could not pull its head inside, so its neck was protected by bony spines, and its tail ended in a spiked club. It had a toothless beak, yet small teeth still grew on the roof of its mouth, a leftover from its ancestors.

A small lizard-like reptile, its body only about 15 cm long, known from a single partial skeleton from the Triassic Madygen Formation of Kyrgyzstan, about 230 million years ago. A row of long, hockey-stick-shaped appendages, each longer than its body, grew from its back; they are usually reconstructed as a fan of display plumes. It was once wrongly claimed to be a feathered ancestor of birds, and its relationships among reptiles are still uncertain. It probably climbed in trees and caught insects.

A tiny gliding reptile, about 25 cm long including its long tail, from the Triassic Madygen Formation of Kyrgyzstan, about 230 million years ago. Unlike any other known glider, its main wing was a skin membrane stretched between its very long hind legs and the base of its tail, forming a delta wing, with perhaps a smaller membrane in front. It probably glided between trees around a lake, catching insects.

A giraffe-necked reptile up to about 6 metres long from the Middle Triassic of Monte San Giorgio on the Swiss-Italian border, about 242 million years ago. Its stiff neck, made of only 13 enormously long vertebrae, was longer than its body and tail together. With nostrils on top of its snout and long, interlocking fangs, it lived in shallow coastal water as an ambush hunter of fish and squid-like animals. The fossils of a smaller relative from the same rocks, Tanystropheus longobardicus, were long mistaken for its young.

A long-necked marine reptile about 3-4 metres long from the Middle Triassic Muschelkalk sea of Germany, about 240 million years ago, and an early relative of the plesiosaurs. Its long, flat skull held a trap of long, outward-pointing fangs for catching fish, and it swam with webbed, paddle-like limbs and waves of its long tail. Like a seal, it could probably haul itself out onto the shore to rest.

A stocky marine reptile about 2 metres long from the Middle Triassic seas of Germany, about 243 million years ago. It plucked shellfish from the sea floor with its forward-pointing front teeth and crushed them with broad, flat tooth plates on its jaws and palate. Its heavy, dense bones acted as ballast, and a row of bony knobs ran down its back. It swam slowly with its long tail and short, paddle-like limbs.

A turtle-like placodont about 1 metre long from the Late Triassic lagoon deposits of Tübingen, Germany, about 230 million years ago. Its body was covered by a very flat, almost rectangular shell, wider than it was long, made of a mosaic of small bony plates. Its boxy head ended in a broad, square, almost toothless snout, which may have carried baleen-like structures for straining food or horny plates for grazing algae. Unlike other placodonts it seems to have lived in brackish water.

A strange marine reptile about 3 metres long from the Middle Triassic of Luoping in Yunnan, China, about 245 million years ago, and one of the earliest known plant-eating marine reptiles. Its jaws widened at the front into a hammerhead shape lined with chisel-like teeth, used to scrape algae off rocks, with many tiny needle-like teeth behind to filter it from the water. It was first described in 2014 with a zip-like split snout; better skulls found later revealed the hammerhead.

One of the largest amphibians that ever lived, up to about 5 metres long, from the Middle Triassic lakes and deltas of southern Germany, about 240 million years ago. Its huge, flat, triangular skull was over a metre long, with eyes on top and two big tusks in the lower jaw whose tips poked up through holes in the snout. With its small limbs and flattened body it lived in the water like a giant salamander, ambushing fish and other animals.

A large, flat-bodied amphibian about 2 metres long from the Late Triassic of Krasiejów in southern Poland, about 228 million years ago, where hundreds of its bones have been found. Its broad, flat skull had its eyes set unusually far forward, and its short limbs were too weak to carry it far on land. It lay on the bottoms of rivers and lakes, snapping up fish; mass graves of its relatives suggest they crowded together in drying pools.

A small, common ichthyosaur about 1 metre long from the Middle Triassic of Monte San Giorgio on the Swiss-Italian border and elsewhere, about 242 million years ago. Fossils with traces of soft tissue show it had a tall dorsal fin, one of the earliest in an ichthyosaur, and its tail had a downward bend with a lower lobe. It is often seen as a halfway stage between eel-like early ichthyosaurs and the fast, tuna-shaped later ones, and it hunted fish and squid-like animals with its long, toothed snout.

A colossal early ichthyosaur about 17 metres long from the 246-million-year-old rocks of the Augusta Mountains in Nevada, described in 2021. Its skull alone was about 2 metres long, making it the first giant animal of the oceans, which reached whale size less than three million years after the first ichthyosaurs appeared. Unlike later ichthyosaurs it had a long, slender, eel-like body with no tall dorsal fin and only a gentle tail fin, and it hunted squid-like animals, fish and perhaps smaller marine reptiles.

A Middle Triassic ammonoid from the Muschelkalk sea of Germany, about 240 million years ago, with a shell about 10 cm across. Its flat-sided shell is crossed by strong ribs that swell into knobs at the edge of the broad, flat outer rim. It gave its name to the 'ceratitic' sutures, the lines where the chamber walls meet the shell, with smooth rounded saddles and finely toothed lobes. Ceratitid ammonoids flourished in the Triassic seas, and almost all died out at its end.

The commonest large predator of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of the western United States, about 155-150 million years old. Adults reached about 8.5 metres, with a long, narrow skull bearing a short horn in front of each eye and a low ridge along each side of the snout. Rather than a crushing bite, it probably struck with its upper jaw like a hatchet, slicing with serrated teeth. Wounds on Stegosaurus and Allosaurus bones record fights between the two.

A Late Jurassic predator of the Morrison Formation, about 6 metres long, that shared its world with the larger Allosaurus. It had a blade-like horn on its nose, a low hornlet over each eye, extraordinarily long upper teeth and four fingers on short arms. Unusually for a theropod, a single row of small bony osteoderms ran down the middle of its back. Its deep, flexible tail has led some to suggest it hunted fish and other prey in wetlands.

One of the largest predators of the Early Jurassic, about 7 metres long, from the Kayenta Formation of Arizona, around 190 million years old. It is named for the pair of thin, half-moon crests along the top of its skull, probably used for display. A notch behind the narrow snout tip gave its upper jaw a kinked profile. The frill and venom of the Jurassic Park film are fiction; its real skull was strong and its teeth suited to large prey.

A small, lightly built theropod about one metre long, much of it tail, from the Late Jurassic lagoons of Bavaria and southern France, about 150 million years old. For over a century it was the smallest dinosaur known. Its long hind legs made it a fast runner, and the first skeleton has a whole lizard, Bavarisaurus, preserved in its stomach. Close relatives had a coat of simple filament feathers.

An early tyrannosauroid, a distant relative of Tyrannosaurus, about 3 metres long, from the Shishugou Formation of Xinjiang in China, about 160 million years old. Its name means 'crowned dragon', after the tall, thin, fan-like crest running along the middle of its snout. Unlike its giant descendants it had long, three-fingered arms. Two skeletons were found together in a pit, possibly mired in a bog formed by a sauropod footprint.

The best-known plated dinosaur, about 9 metres long, from the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of North America, about 155-150 million years old. Two staggered rows of broad bony plates ran down its arched back, probably for display, and four long spikes at the end of its tail made a formidable weapon. Its hind legs were far longer than its front legs, so it carried its tiny, narrow head close to the ground. It cropped low plants with a horny beak.

A stegosaur about 4.5 metres long from the Late Jurassic Tendaguru beds of Tanzania, about 152 million years old. Pairs of narrow plates on its neck and shoulders gave way to pairs of long, sharp spikes along its hips and tail, and a long spike jutted back from each shoulder. Studies of its tail suggest it could swing the spikes fast enough to inflict deep wounds. Over a thousand of its bones were found, though many were destroyed in Berlin during the Second World War.

One of the earliest armoured dinosaurs, about 4 metres long, from Early Jurassic rocks around 190 million years old near Charmouth in Dorset. It walked on all fours, with rows of oval, keeled bony scutes along its neck, back, flanks and tail, an early version of the armour of stegosaurs and ankylosaurs. Its skeleton, described by Richard Owen in the 1860s, was the first near-complete dinosaur ever found. It cropped plants with a small beak and leaf-shaped teeth.

A long, slender sauropod of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation, about 154-152 million years old, reaching about 25 metres from snout to tail tip. Its very long neck was held out nearly level, letting it sweep across wide areas of ferns and horsetails, and its even longer tail tapered into a thin whiplash. Its small head had peg-like teeth only at the front of the jaws, used to strip leaves from branches. Casts of the skeleton nicknamed 'Dippy' stand in museums around the world.

A Late Jurassic sauropod from Sichuan in China, about 22 metres long, with one of the longest necks of any animal relative to its body. The neck made up nearly half its length and was built from 19 long, lightweight vertebrae braced by bony rods. It probably browsed over a wide arc of vegetation without moving its body. Its fossils come from river and lake deposits about 160 million years old.

A pigeon-sized scansoriopterygid dinosaur from rocks about 160 million years old in Hebei, China, described in 2015. Instead of feathered wings it had bat-like wings of skin stretched between its very long third finger and a long rod of bone at the wrist, a structure unknown in any other dinosaur. Its body was covered in filament-like feathers. It probably climbed trees and glided between them, an experiment in flight that left no descendants.

A crow-sized feathered dinosaur from western Liaoning, China, about 160 million years old, slightly older than Archaeopteryx. It had long flight feathers on its legs as well as its arms, giving it four wings. Melanosomes preserved in its feathers revealed its colours: a grey body, white wing feathers with black tips and a rufous crest. Pellets found with its skeletons contain lizard bones and fish scales, showing what it ate.

A long-tailed pterosaur from the Late Jurassic Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, about 150 million years old, with a wingspan of up to about 1.8 metres. Its long jaws held needle-like, forward-pointing teeth for catching fish, and its stiff tail ended in a diamond-shaped vane. Some fossils preserve fish in its throat, and one is locked in the jaws of the large fish Aspidorhynchus, which seized it as it skimmed the water.

An early pterosaur from the Early Jurassic cliffs of Lyme Regis in Dorset, about 195 million years old, first found by Mary Anning in 1828. It had a wingspan of about 1.4 metres and an enormous, deep skull lightened by large openings, carrying two kinds of teeth: long fangs at the front and small ones behind. Its short wings and strong claws suggest it was a poor long-distance flier that climbed well and snatched small animals on land.

The oldest known gliding mammal, a squirrel-sized animal from the Daohugou beds of Inner Mongolia, about 164-159 million years old. A furry skin membrane stretched between its front and hind limbs, preserved with hair impressions, and its long, flattened tail acted as a stabiliser. It belonged to the eutriconodonts, an extinct group of early mammals. Its sharp, pointed teeth suggest a diet of insects.

A semi-aquatic docodont, a close relative of true mammals, from Middle Jurassic lake deposits about 164 million years old in Inner Mongolia. About 45 cm long, it had dense fur, webbed, sprawling limbs for swimming and digging, and a broad, flat, scaly tail like a beaver's. Its recurved, seal-like teeth were suited to gripping fish and aquatic invertebrates. It showed that mammal relatives had taken to the water far earlier than once thought.

A long-necked plesiosaur about 4 metres long from the Middle Jurassic Oxford Clay of England, about 165 million years old. Its small, flat head carried many long, thin, interlocking teeth that formed a trap for small fish and squid-like cephalopods. It swam by 'flying' through the water with four long, pointed flippers. Many fine skeletons were dug from brick pits around Peterborough.

A fully marine relative of crocodiles, about 3 metres long, from the Middle to Late Jurassic seas of Europe, about 165-160 million years old. It had lost the bony armour of its land cousins and had paddle-like limbs and a shark-like tail fin with the larger lobe pointing down. Its long, narrow snout held conical teeth for catching fish and cephalopods. Salt glands in its head let it live at sea without fresh water.

A large marine crocodyliform, about 4-5 metres long, from Late Jurassic seas of Europe, about 157-145 million years old. Unlike its slender-snouted relatives it had a short, deep snout lined with large, serrated, blade-like teeth, earning a related species the nickname 'Godzilla'. It was a top predator able to cut up large prey such as marine reptiles. Like other metriorhynchids it had paddle limbs and a downturned tail fin.

A hybodont shark about 2 metres long from the Early Jurassic Posidonia Shale of Holzmaden, Germany, about 182 million years old. Hybodonts were a long-lived side branch of the sharks, with a stout, grooved bony spine in front of each of their two dorsal fins and a mix of pointed and crushing teeth. One famous skeleton has the remains of about 250 belemnites in its stomach. Males carried hooked spines on the head, probably used in mating.

A heavily armoured ray-finned fish of the Early Jurassic, a relative of today's gars, about one metre long. Its body was covered in thick, shiny, diamond-shaped ganoid scales set in diagonal rows. Rows of button-like teeth in its small mouth crushed snails and shellfish, and its fossils are common in the Toarcian rocks of Germany and England. Such teeth were once sold as 'toadstones', believed to protect against poison.

An ammonite of the Early Jurassic Toarcian seas, about 180 million years old, so widespread and short-lived that it marks a zone of time across Europe. Its flat, widely coiled shell, up to about 10 cm across, has a sharp keel flanked by two grooves, a smooth spiral groove along the middle of each side and sickle-shaped ribs on the outer half. It is named after St Hilda of Whitby, where its fossils are common. Legend said they were snakes turned to stone by the saint.

A sea lily of the Early Jurassic, about 195 million years old, that lived not on the seabed but hanging from floating driftwood in the open sea. Long, five-sided stems ringed with tendrils held crowns of densely branched, feathery arms that strained plankton from the water. At Lyme Regis in Dorset whole masses of them are preserved tangled around fossil logs. When the waterlogged wood finally sank, the colony died with it.

A horseshoe crab from the Late Jurassic Solnhofen lagoons of Bavaria, about 150 million years old, very like the living Limulus. It had a broad, domed head shield with compound eyes, a spiny hinged rear shield and a long, spike-like tail used to steer and flip itself over. Horseshoe crabs are chelicerates, closer to spiders and scorpions than to true crabs. One famous slab shows a Mesolimulus dead at the end of its own trackway, which it left as it wandered into the toxic lagoon floor.

A large prawn, around 15-20 cm long, from the Late Jurassic Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, about 150 million years old.
